(p-693) Sūrat "al-Ikhlāṣ" (The Sincerity)

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Say: He is Allah, the One.﴾ "Huwa" (He) is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n), and "Allahu aḥad" (Allah is One) is the matter itself, like your saying: "He is Zayd, departing (munṭalliq)." It is as if it were said: "The matter is this, namely that Allah is One, having no second." The place of "huwa" is nominative (raf') as the subject (mubtada'), and the predicate is the sentence. It does not require a returning pronoun (rājiʿ), because it is in the sense of a singular noun, as in your saying: "Zayd is your servant (ghulāmuka)," in that it is the subject in meaning. That is because His saying "Allahu aḥad" is the matter which is an expression of it. This is not the case with "Zayd, his father is departing," for "Zayd" and the sentence indicate two different meanings, so something must connect them.

It is related from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, that: "The Quraysh said: O Muhammad, describe for us your Lord to whom you invite us. So it was revealed..." meaning: "The One you asked me to describe is Allah (Exalted)." On this reading, "aḥad" is the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "He is One (aḥad)," and it has the meaning of "wāḥid" (one). Its origin is "waḥad," and the wāw was changed to a hamza because it occurred at the end of the word.

The rational proof that He is One is that the one either is sufficient for the management and creation of the world, or is not. If it is sufficient, then the other is superfluous, not needed, and that is a deficiency; and what is deficient cannot be a god. If it is not sufficient, then it is deficient. Also, reason requires that the created thing needs an agent, and one agent is sufficient; and beyond one, there is no reason for one number to be preferred over another, so this leads to the existence of infinite numbers, and that is impossible. Thus the claim that there are two gods is impossible. Also, one of them either is able to conceal some of its acts from the other, or is not able. If it is able, it follows that the one concealed from is ignorant; and if it is not able, it follows that it is incapable. Also, if we suppose a possible existent that does not exist, then if neither of them is able to bring it into being, each of them is incapable, and the incapable cannot be a god. If one of them is able and the other is not, the other cannot be a god. If both are able, then either they bring it into being by cooperation, so each of them needs the help of the other, and thus each is incapable; or each is able to bring it into being independently, and then when one of them brings it into being, either the second remains able to bring it into being, which is impossible, because bringing into being what already exists is impossible; or it does not remain able, and then the first has nullified the power of the second, so the second is incapable and subdued under his disposal, and thus is not a god. If you say: "When the one brings into being something that is within its power by itself, its power has ceased, so it follows for you that this one has made itself incapable," we say: "When the one brings into being what is within its own power, its power has been fully executed, and whoever's power is fully executed is not incapable. As for the partner, his power has not been executed, but has ceased because of the power of the other, and that is incapacitation."

Allah, the Eternal Refuge (al-Samad). It is on the pattern "fa'al" in the sense of "maf'ul" (passive participle), from "samada ilayhi" (صَمَدَ إلَيْهِ), meaning he directed himself to him, i.e. intended him. He is the Master (al-sayyid) to whom one turns in needs. The meaning is: He is Allah whom you know, and whom you acknowledge as the Creator of the heavens and the earth and your Creator. He is One, with no partner. He is the One to whom every creature turns, none of them being independent of Him, and He is the One who is free of need of them.

﴿He neither begets﴾, because He is not of a kind that could be paired, so that He would have a consort of His own kind and they would beget offspring. This meaning is indicated by His saying: ﴿How can He have a son when He has no consort?﴾ [al-An'am: 101]. ﴿Nor is He begotten﴾, because every begotten thing is originated (muhdath) and a body (jism), whereas He is eternal (qadim), having no beginning to His existence. For if He were not eternal, He would be originated, since there is no intermediary between the two. And if He were originated, He would require an originator, and likewise the second, and the third, which leads to an infinite regress (tasalsul), and that is invalid. And He is not a body, because "body" is the name for something composed of parts. In that case, either each part of it would possess the attributes of perfection, so that each part would be a god, and the belief would be corrupted just as it is corrupted by [the belief in] two gods; or it would not possess them, but rather their opposites, the marks of origination, and that is impossible. (p-695)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 112, verse 4:

﴿And there is none comparable to Him, any one.﴾ That is, no one equals Him or is like Him. They asked him to describe his Lord for them, so there was revealed to him what contains His attributes (exalted is He). His saying, "He is Allah," is an indication that He is the Creator of things and their Originator. Implicit in this is the description of Him as Capable and Knowing, because the Creator necessarily requires power and knowledge, given that creation is established upon the utmost precision, harmony and order. Included in this is the description of Him as Living, because whoever is characterized by power and knowledge must necessarily be living. Included in this too is the description of Him as All-Hearing, All-Seeing, Willing, Speaking, and other attributes of perfection, since if He were not described by them He would be described by their opposites, which are deficiencies, and these are signs of createdness (hadath). Therefore it is impossible for the Eternal (al-Qadim) to be characterized by them. His saying, "One (Ahad)," is a description of His oneness (wahdaniyya), of the negation of a partner, and of His being the sole One who originates the non-existent and the sole One who knows the hidden things. His saying, "The Self-Sufficient Master (al-Samad)," is a description of Him as one who is in no way in need, but to whom everything is in need. Since He is not in need of anything, He is self-sufficient (Ghani), needing no one, while everyone needs Him. His saying, "He begets not," is a negation of resemblance and of homogeneity. His saying, "nor is He begotten," is a negation of origination (huduth) and a description of Him as eternal (qidam) and primordial (awwaliyya). His saying, "And there is none comparable to Him," is a negation that anything resembles Him. Whoever claims that the negation of the equal (kufu', which means the like) applies to the past and does not indicate its negation for the present, while the disbelievers claim it for the present, has strayed in his error. For if it was not so in the past, it is necessarily not so in the present, since what is created cannot be an equal to the Eternal. The ultimate content of the disbelievers' speech amounts to polytheism (ishrak), anthropomorphism (tashbih), and denial of attributes (ta'til), and the surah repels all of them, as we have established.

Sibawayh regarded as good the fronting of the adverbial complement (al-zarf) when it is stable (mustaqirr), i.e., a predicate (khabar), because since it is what is needed, it is fronted so that it is known from the outset that it is a predicate and not a superfluous element (fadla). Its postponement, when it is lagha (i.e., a superfluous element, fadla), is because postponement is the deserved position of superfluous elements. It was fronted in the more eloquent utterance (p-696) because the statement is directed toward negating equality from the essence of the Originator, may He be glorified, and the locus and center of this meaning is this complement, so fronting it is the more important.

Abu 'Amr used to prefer pausing on "Ahad" and not joining it. 'Abd al-Warith said: "Upon this we found the reciters." When joining, one pronounces it with tanwin and kasra, or omits the tanwin, as in the reading of ﴿'Uzayrun ibnu Allah﴾ [al-Tawba: 30]. "Kufu'" with a sukun on the fa' and with hamza is the reading of Hamza and Khalaf. "Kufwan," with a heavy (mushaddad) letter and without hamza, is the reading of Hafs. The rest read it heavy and with hamza.

In a hadith: "Whoever recites Surah al-Ikhlas has recited a third of the Qur'an," because the Qur'an comprises the oneness of Allah, the mention of His attributes, commands and prohibitions, stories and admonitions, and this surah is entirely devoted to tawhid and the attributes, so it contains a third of the Qur'an. In this is evidence of the nobility of the science of tawhid. And how could it not be so, when a science is ennobled by the nobility of its object and made lowly by its lowliness? The object of this science is Allah, His attributes, what is permissible for Him and what is impermissible for Him. So what do you think of the nobility of its station and the greatness of its place?! O Allah, gather us among those who know You, who act for You, who hope for Your reward, who fear Your punishment, and who are honored with meeting You. "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) heard a man reciting, 'Say: He is Allah, One,' and he said, 'It is incumbent (wajabat),' and it was asked, 'O Messenger of Allah, what is incumbent?' He said, 'Paradise has become incumbent upon him.'"
